summary: NPR Planet Money article by Paddy Hirsch (April 5, 2022) explaining how the Russian ruble, which fell about 40% after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, recovered to become the world's top-performing currency in March despite sanctions. It attributes the recovery to holes in the sanctions (European natural gas purchases, oil prices, trade with China and India, the sovereign debt carve-out), and to internal government measures such as a 20% interest rate, forced currency conversion of exporters' revenue, a ban on selling foreign-owned securities, and limits on transfers abroad. The article argues this is a manufactured 'Potemkin currency' with serious risks, especially if Putin's demand for ruble payment for gas forces buyers to renegotiate contracts and turn to other suppliers.
one_line: NPR Planet Money explains how sanctions holes and Russian government measures pushed the ruble to a sharp recovery after the Ukraine invasion, and why it is fragile.
key_facts: The Russian ruble was down 40%, at 139 rubles to the dollar, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, at its low point on March 7.
At the time of writing, the ruble was trading at 84 to the dollar, right back where it was at the time of the invasion.
The ruble was the world's top-performing currency in March.
Russia holds about $640 billion worth of euros, dollars, yen and other foreign currencies in banks around the world, about half of it in the U.S. and Europe.
The U.S. Treasury left a window open to allow financial intermediaries to process sovereign debt interest payments for Russia; that window was scheduled to close this month.
On Feb. 28, the Central Bank of Russia increased interest rates to 20%.
Russian businesses must swap 80% of money they make overseas into rubles.
The Kremlin issued an edict banning Russian brokers from selling securities owned by foreigners.
Conversions of hard currency for individuals are limited to $10,000 through the end of the year.
Putin told certain buyers of Russian natural gas that they must pay their gas bills in rubles, which the article says would force buyers to buy large amounts of rubles.
The article describes the recovery as a 'Potemkin currency,' referring to Grigory Potemkin, governor of Crimea after Catherine the Great annexed it in 1784.
Elvira Nabiullina is the head of the Central Bank of Russia.
The Russian economy is already expected to contract by more than 8% this year.
Russia is the world's biggest exporter of natural gas, according to a correction added April 8, 2022; an earlier version wrongly called it the biggest producer.
Alternative gas supply ideas mentioned include the U.S., the U.K., Norway, Qatar, Azerbaijan, and an Israeli pipeline idea.
